passages.text: This same man, who alone was a true prophet, appropriately assigned names to each living creature according to the worth of its nature, as did the one who made it. For if he gave anything a name, that was also the name given by the maker to what had come into being. Why, then, did he still need to partake of a plant, so that he might see just what good or evil is? “He was commanded.” But the undiscerning believe these things, supposing that an irrational beast had become more beneficent than God, who created both them and everything.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the worth of its nature
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves ἀξία as worth or corresponding value; “according to the character appropriate to its nature” is a smoother alternative.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as did the one who made it
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes the clause as elliptically repeating the act of naming, supported by the following sentence. It could instead compare the suitable naming with how the maker formed the creature.

lexical_decisions.chosen: did he still need to partake of a plant
lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive φυτοῦ is retained without supplying an explicit fruit; προσλαβεῖν can denote taking or partaking.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He was commanded
lexical_decisions.rationale: The middle-passive form is read passively with the man as recipient of the command. As a deponent middle it could alternatively mean “he was commanding.”

passages.text: Nevertheless, a female nature was jointly created as a mate for this man, falling far short of him, as participation falls short of essence, as the moon of the sun, as fire of light. She, ruling as a female over the present world, which is like her, is believed to be the first prophetess, professing prophecy along with all those “among those born of women.” But the other, being male as “Son of Man,” also prophesies the superior things, as befits a male, for the age to come.

lexical_decisions.chosen: as participation falls short of essence
lexical_decisions.rationale: Carries forward the idea of falling short from ἀποδέουσα; the compact philosophical contrast is literally “as participation of essence.”

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῦ νῦν κόσμου ὡς θήλεια ὁμοίου ἄρχουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: ruling as a female over the present world, which is like her
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes ὁμοίου with κόσμου and supplies the contextually implicit standard of likeness. An alternative is “ruling as a female over the corresponding present world.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: professing prophecy
lexical_decisions.rationale: Here ἐπαγγέλλομαι can mean professing or laying claim to something, not only promising it.

lexical_decisions.chosen: the superior things
lexical_decisions.rationale: διαφέροντα can denote things that excel, fitting the contrast between the present and coming ages; “the things that differ” remains possible.

source_issues.issue: The printed hyphen immediately before αὐτοῦ is anomalous and appears to be stray punctuation or a line-break artifact. The translation treats αὐτοῦ as the complement of ἀποδέουσα.

source_issues.source_quote: ὡς ἡλίου σελήνη; ὡς φωτὸς τὸ πῦρ
source_issues.issue: The printed Greek question mark interrupts a continuing series of comparisons and is likely an editorial punctuation error. The translation punctuates the comparisons continuously.
source_issues.proposed_reading: ὡς ἡλίου σελήνη, ὡς φωτὸς τὸ πῦρ

passages.text: Let there be, then, two generic prophecies for us: the masculine one (and let it be specified that the first, being male, has thereafter been placed second according to the principle of progression, whereas the second, being female, was appointed to come first in the procession of the pairs)—the one, then, who is “among those born of women,” making promises as the female belonging to the present world, wants to be believed to be masculine. Therefore, stealing the male’s seeds and covering them with her own seeds of the flesh, she brings forth the offspring together as though they were all her own—that is, the words. And she promises to give present earthly wealth as a dowry, wishing to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἡ μὲν ἀρσενικὴ ... ἡ μὲν οὖν
lexical_decisions.chosen: the masculine one ... the one, then
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the Greek construction’s interruption and resumption around the parenthesis rather than supplying a new contrast absent from the source.

lexical_decisions.chosen: according to the principle of progression
lexical_decisions.rationale: λόγος denotes the governing principle or rationale, while πρόοδος describes progression or procession.

lexical_decisions.chosen: in the procession of the pairs
lexical_decisions.rationale: συζυγίαι are paired counterparts; “sequence of the pairs” is also possible for προέλευσις.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοῖς ἰδίοις τῆς σαρκὸς σπέρμασιν ἐπισκέπτουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: covering them with her own seeds of the flesh
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπισκέπτω here has the sense of covering over; the pronoun “them” represents the previously mentioned male seeds.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τῷ ταχεῖ τὸ βραδύ, τὸ βραχὺ τῷ μείζονι ὑπαλλάξαι
lexical_decisions.chosen: to exchange the slow for the quick, the brief for the greater
lexical_decisions.rationale: Treats the accusatives as what is exchanged for the dative counterparts. The direction of exchange can be construed in reverse with ὑπαλλάσσω, but this rendering follows the most direct case pattern.

passages.text: Yet she not only dares to speak and hear of many gods, but also believes that she herself will become one; and in the hope of becoming what she does not have by nature, she also destroys what she does have. And as a female, when she enters her menstrual periods, she is stained with blood under the pretext of sacrifices and so defiles those who touch her. And whenever, after conceiving, she gives birth to temporary kings, she stirs up wars that shed much blood. As for those who long to learn truth from her, by saying everything in contradictory ways and providing many and various services, she puts them in a state of always seeking and finding nothing until death itself. For from the beginning she has lain before blind people as an occasion of death; by prophesying deceptive, ambiguous, and crooked things, she deceives those who believe.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἐλπίδι τοῦ γενέσθαι ὃ μὴ ἔχει φύσιν καὶ ὃ ἔχει προσαπολλύουσα
lexical_decisions.chosen: in the hope of becoming what she does not have by nature, she also destroys what she does have
lexical_decisions.rationale: Reads φύσιν adverbially with the first ἔχει and preserves the contrast between what she lacks and possesses. A more impersonal alternative is “becoming what has no nature and destroying what does.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: when she enters her menstrual periods
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐμμήνια denotes menstruation or menstrual discharge; the wording preserves the author’s female-body imagery.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τοὺς αἷμα πολὺ χέοντας ἐγείρει πολέμους
lexical_decisions.chosen: she stirs up wars that shed much blood
lexical_decisions.rationale: Attaches the masculine participial phrase to the adjacent πολέμους. It could instead describe the kings as shedding much blood, followed by the separate statement that she stirs up wars.

lexical_decisions.chosen: providing many and various services
lexical_decisions.rationale: ὑπουργία denotes service or assistance; “requirements of service” is possible if the phrase refers to tasks imposed on seekers.

lexical_decisions.chosen: has lain ... as an occasion of death
lexical_decisions.rationale: πρόφασις can mean pretext, occasion, or ostensible cause; “occasion” best fits death as the resulting harm.

passages.text: Therefore she imposed an equivocal name on her firstborn, calling him Cain, which admits a twofold interpretation; for it is interpreted both as “possession” and as “jealousy,” since in what was to come he was destined to be jealous of him over either a wife or possessions or the parents’ affection for him. But if none of these things actually came about, even so, calling him “possession” has hit the mark well; for she acquired him first, and this also proved useful to her. For he was a “murderer” and “liar,” and, with his sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling. Moreover, those who came from his line became the first adulterers; they fashioned harps and lyres and became smiths of weapons of war. Therefore the prophecy of the descendants too, full of adulterers and harps, secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures, as it were.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: ἀμφοτερίζον ... ὃ διχῇ ἔχει τῆς ἑρμηνείας τὴν ἐκδοχήν
lexical_decisions.chosen: equivocal ... which admits a twofold interpretation
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἀμφοτερίζον describes something that goes in both directions or bears two senses, which the following clause explicitly identifies.

lexical_decisions.chosen: he was destined to be jealous of him
lexical_decisions.rationale: Preserves the unresolved masculine pronoun rather than identifying its referent as Abel; ζηλόω may also mean being zealous for or emulating someone, though jealousy suits the listed causes.

lexical_decisions.chosen: calling him “possession” has hit the mark well
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἐπιτυγχάνω conveys attaining or hitting the mark; the infinitive phrase functions as the subject.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: μετὰ ἁμαρτιῶν ἡσυχάζειν μηδὲ ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν θέλων
lexical_decisions.chosen: with his sins, was unwilling to live quietly even while ruling
lexical_decisions.rationale: Takes μετά as accompaniment and ἐπὶ τῷ ἄρχειν temporally. Alternatives include “after his sins” and “even for the sake of ruling.”

lexical_decisions.chosen: they fashioned harps and lyres
lexical_decisions.rationale: ἁρμόζω can mean fitting together, constructing, or tuning; “fashioned” fits the account of originating instruments without excluding tuning.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: λανθανόντως διὰ τῶν ἡδυπαθειῶν ὡς τοὺς πολέμους ἐγείρει
lexical_decisions.chosen: secretly stirs up wars through sensual pleasures, as it were
lexical_decisions.rationale: λανθανόντως denotes acting unnoticed or covertly, while ὡς is taken as qualifying the assertion with “as it were.” It could alternatively be read as “somehow” or exclamatorily as “how ...!”
